chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya from Muhammad ibn Ahmad from Musa ibn Ja'far al-Baghdadi from Ja'far ibn Yahya from Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman from al-Husayn ibn Zayd from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from his father (peace be upon him) who said:

Umar ibn al-Khattab was brought Qudama ibn Maz'un, and he had drunk wine. So two men testified against him, one of them was a eunuch (castrated) and he was Amr al-Tameemi, and the other was al-Mu'alla ibn al-Jarud. So one of them testified that he saw him drinking, and the other testified that he saw him vomiting the wine.

So Umar sent for some people from the companions of the Messenger of Allah, among them was the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him). So he said to the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him), 'What do you say, O Abu al-Hasan, for you are the one regarding whom the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: You are the most knowledgeable of this community and its judge with the truth. For these two have differed in their testimonies.'
He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no difference in their testimonies, and he could not have vomited it until he had drunk it.'
So he said, 'Is the testimony of the eunuch allowed?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'The loss of his beard is not except like the loss of some of his limbs.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on the testimony of a eunuch and how did Imam Ali resolve the discrepancy in the witnesses' accounts of Qudama drinking wine?
ai.summary: This hadith highlights the jurisprudential acumen of Imam Ali (AS) during the Umayyad period, demonstrating how he resolved conflicting witness testimonies by establishing a causal link between drinking and vomiting, thereby validating both accounts. It also provides a nuanced legal precedent regarding the validity of a eunuch's testimony, with Imam Ali reasoning that the absence of a beard does not equate to the absence of other essential physical attributes required for legal capacity. This narration underscores the continuity of prophetic wisdom in early Islamic legal practice and the respect accorded to Imam Ali as the foremost jurist of the community.
